introduction: This fourth Sunday of Lent is Laetare Sunday, and rose vestments may be worn. The people of Israel celebrate the Passover in the promised land. In the Gospel, Jesus tells the parable of the father who runs to welcome his lost son, and who goes out to plead with the elder son as well. Paul urges us: be reconciled to God. Let us rejoice in the Father's mercy.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God reconciled the world to himself in Christ. Let us bring our prayers to the merciful Father.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be like the father in the parable, running to welcome every sinner who returns. Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests who hear confessions: that they may be faithful ambassadors of God's reconciliation. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are far from home, from their families or from God: that they may come to themselves and return. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who, like the elder son, are resentful or feel unappreciated: that they may rejoice in God's mercy to others. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may be reconciled to God and to one another before Easter. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful Father, you run to meet us when we return to you. Give us the grace to come home, and teach us to rejoice when others come home too. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: He was lost and is found
reflection.body:
The tax collectors and sinners are coming close to listen to Jesus, and the religious leaders grumble: "This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them." Jesus answers with one of his best-loved parables.

A younger son demands his inheritance, leaves home and wastes everything. When famine comes, he ends up feeding pigs and longing to eat their food. Then "he came to himself." He decides to go home and say, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son."

But the father has been watching: "while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him." The son hardly gets to finish his speech. The father calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals and a feast, "for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found."

There is a second son, who has stayed at home and worked hard. When he hears the music, he is angry and refuses to go in. And again the father comes out, this time to plead with him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours." The parable ends without telling us whether he went in. Jesus leaves the question open for us.

Paul gives us the meaning: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses." And he pleads with us: "we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God."

This is why Laetare Sunday is joyful. We may be the younger son, far from home, or the elder son, near but resentful. Either way, the Father comes out to meet us. This week, go to confession and let the Father embrace you. And if someone has come back whom you find hard to welcome, go in to the feast.
